items.prompt: What does 'right-sizing' mean in this unit's terms?
choices: Provisioning a resource's capacity to match measured usage plus a deliberate safety margin, instead of a guessed-high number
Always choosing the smallest instance size available, regardless of usage
Buying a fixed amount of cloud capacity once and never changing it
A billing discount cloud providers give for using less compute
items.explanation: Right-sizing is about matching provisioned capacity to actual, measured usage with deliberate headroom — not blindly minimizing size, and not a provider discount.
items.reference:
📏 Right-sizing = measured usage + deliberate margin
🙈 'Just in case' sizing = guessed margin, never revisited

Why: The gap between a guess and a measurement is where waste hides.

items.prompt: In the Scenario, staging was provisioned for '4x normal load, just in case.' What did measuring actual usage reveal?
choices: Actual peak need was only about 1.2x normal load, meaning the environment was massively over-provisioned
Actual usage exceeded 4x normal load, so the sizing was correct
Usage couldn't be measured at all
Staging used exactly 4x normal load every single day
items.explanation: Once measured, staging's real peak need was around 1.2x normal load — far below the 4x guess used to justify its original sizing, which is exactly the gap right-sizing is meant to close.
items.reference:
📏 Right-sizing = measured usage + deliberate margin
🙈 'Just in case' sizing = guessed margin, never revisited

Why: The gap between a guess and a measurement is where waste hides.

items.prompt: Why is right-sizing described as a loop rather than a one-time exercise?
choices: Because usage patterns drift over time, so a sizing decision made once and never revisited quietly goes stale
Because cloud providers require resizing every month by policy
Because measuring usage is impossible to do more than once
Because right-sizing only applies to brand-new resources
items.explanation: A right-sizing decision reflects usage at the moment it was measured; as traffic, team size, or the product itself changes, the same sizing can become wrong again, which is why re-auditing periodically is part of the loop, not an optional extra.
items.reference:
📏 Right-sizing = measured usage + deliberate margin
🙈 'Just in case' sizing = guessed margin, never revisited

Why: The gap between a guess and a measurement is where waste hides.

items.prompt: Which of L1's three waste sources is 'forgotten test databases' an example of?
choices: Idle/forgotten resources — still running and billing after the project that justified them ended
Unbounded auto-scaling
A billing error on the cloud provider's side
Over-provisioned production sizing
items.explanation: Test databases left running after their project ended are the idle/forgotten resources pattern — capacity nobody is actively using but that keeps billing anyway.
items.reference:
🗑️ Idle/forgotten — still billing after the need ended
🛡️ 'Just in case' — sized above measured need, never revisited
📈 Unbounded autoscale — no ceiling on cost during a spike

Why: Naming the pattern is the first step toward a targeted fix.

items.prompt: A team writes a one-time script that deletes every currently-idle test resource. Six months later, a new batch has accumulated. What did the one-time fix miss?
choices: It resolved the current waste but didn't fix the missing process (ownership, expiry tagging, recurring review) that let idle resources accumulate in the first place
Nothing — a one-time cleanup is always sufficient for idle resources
The script should have deleted production resources too
Idle resources can never actually be prevented, only cleaned up after the fact
items.explanation: Treating idle-resource waste as a single incident to clean up, rather than a recurring pattern to prevent, means the underlying gap (no owner, no expiry, no recurring review) stays open and simply refills over time.
items.reference:
🗑️ Idle/forgotten — still billing after the need ended
🛡️ 'Just in case' — sized above measured need, never revisited
📈 Unbounded autoscale — no ceiling on cost during a spike

Why: Naming the pattern is the first step toward a targeted fix.

items.prompt: What specifically makes 'unbounded auto-scaling' a cost risk, distinct from auto-scaling itself?
choices: Having no upper limit on how far it can scale, so a traffic spike, bug, or retry storm can drive cost as high as the cloud account allows
Auto-scaling is always a cost risk, with or without a ceiling
Auto-scaling only ever scales down, never up
It requires manual approval for every scaling event, which is slow
items.explanation: Auto-scaling itself is a reasonable, common pattern; the risk is specifically the missing ceiling — without a maximum, nothing stops a spike (legitimate or bug-induced) from scaling cost to the account's practical limit.
items.reference:
🗑️ Idle/forgotten — still billing after the need ended
🛡️ 'Just in case' — sized above measured need, never revisited
📈 Unbounded autoscale — no ceiling on cost during a spike

Why: The ceiling, not the scaling itself, is what needs fixing.

items.prompt: In L1's Scenario, what triggered the auto-scaling group to scale up and stay up?

A billing configuration change made by finance
items.explanation: The Scenario describes an auto-scaling group with no upper bound that scaled up during a retry storm and never scaled cleanly back down, quietly leaving elevated capacity (and cost) running.
items.reference:
🗑️ Idle/forgotten — still billing after the need ended
🛡️ 'Just in case' — sized above measured need, never revisited
📈 Unbounded autoscale — no ceiling on cost during a spike

items.prompt: Why did it take a finance invoice, rather than the team itself, to notice the tripled cloud bill?
choices: Nothing was proactively watching total spend the way a dashboard or alert watches a resource metric — cost was only visible retroactively, on the invoice

Finance has better monitoring tools than engineering teams ever could
items.explanation: Cost, unlike a CPU spike or an error rate, doesn't page anyone by default — without a deliberately built dashboard, budget, and alert, the running total stays invisible until a bill arrives after the fact.
items.reference:
👀 A resource metric gets watched because someone builds a dashboard for it
🙈 Cost has no such default — it needs the same deliberate tracking

Why: Visibility doesn't happen by accident; it has to be built.

items.prompt: What kind of tooling does this unit say cost visibility needs, to catch a problem before the bill arrives?

items.reference:
👀 A resource metric gets watched because someone builds a dashboard for it
🙈 Cost has no such default — it needs the same deliberate tracking

Why: Visibility doesn't happen by accident; it has to be built.

items.prompt: L1 frames the tripled bill as coming from 'three individually-reasonable decisions,' not one dramatic incident. What's the key implication of that framing?

items.explanation: Small, individually-reasonable over-provisioning decisions, left unexamined and multiplied across many resources and months, is exactly where real cloud bills balloon — which is why ongoing visibility, not a reactive scramble after one big incident, is the actual fix.
items.reference:
➕ Small waste × many resources × long time = a large bill

Right-sizing (cost) is the counterpart of an SLA (reliability) — both are external contractual commitments
Idle resources (cost) is the counterpart of an SLI (reliability) — both are raw measurable signals

🎯 SLO ↔ Budget (a committed ceiling)
🔥 Burn-rate alert ↔ Budget-forecast alert

Why: The same proactive-visibility shape applies to both axes.

🔥 Burn-rate alert ↔ Budget-forecast alert

items.prompt: Staging was originally sized for '4x normal load,' and measured usage really did spike to 3.5x normal load once a quarter during a scheduled load test. Does that justify keeping the 4x sizing permanently?
choices: No — the right-sized answer is to provision for typical day-to-day usage and handle the rare, known spike with a temporary scale-up or a deliberate budgeted exception, not by paying for peak capacity year-round
Yes — any measured peak, however rare, justifies permanent sizing at that level
No, because rare spikes should simply be ignored entirely
Yes, because 3.5x is close enough to 4x that no change is needed
items.explanation: Sizing permanently for a rare, predictable event is the same over-provisioning mistake wearing a more defensible-sounding number — the fix is to size for typical usage and handle the known rare spike deliberately (temporary scale-up or a budgeted exception), not to pay for peak capacity all month.
items.reference:
📊 Size to typical usage, not to a rare annual peak
🎯 Handle rare, known spikes deliberately and temporarily

Why: Sizing to the 99th-percentile case forever is over-provisioning with better PR.

items.prompt: A resource's measured peak utilization is 22%. Why does this unit recommend right-sizing toward a target utilization band (e.g. 65%) rather than sizing exactly to the measured 22% peak?
choices: Sizing to the exact observed peak leaves no headroom for a genuine spike above anything previously measured — a target band builds in deliberate margin
The target band is arbitrary and has no real purpose
Sizing to the exact peak is always cheaper, so the target band exists only to increase cost
22% utilization is too low to be measured accurately, so a band compensates for measurement error
items.explanation: Trimming a resource to exactly its historically observed peak removes all margin for a future spike that exceeds anything seen so far — a target band under 100% keeps deliberate headroom, which is the difference between right-sizing and over-trimming.
items.reference:
📊 Size to typical usage, not to a rare annual peak
🎯 Handle rare, known spikes deliberately and temporarily

Why: Sizing to the 99th-percentile case forever is over-provisioning with better PR.

items.prompt: In the measure -> right-size -> budget-alert -> re-audit loop, what happens if the 're-audit' step is dropped?
choices: The sizing decision quietly goes stale as usage patterns drift, the same way a one-time snapshot loses accuracy over time
Nothing changes — right-sizing only ever needs to happen once per resource
The budget alert automatically re-triggers the measurement step on its own
Dropping re-audit only affects idle resources, not right-sized ones
items.explanation: A right-sizing decision reflects usage at the moment it was measured; without periodically re-measuring, drift in traffic, team size, or the product itself can make a once-correct sizing wrong again without anyone noticing.
items.reference:
🔁 measure → right-size → budget-alert → re-audit → (repeat)

Why: A loop only works if every step, including the repeat, actually happens.

items.prompt: Why does the right-sizing loop put 'set a budget + alert' after right-sizing rather than before it?
choices: The budget and alert are set on the new, right-sized baseline, so they reflect what spend should look like going forward rather than the old, over-provisioned number
Order doesn't matter at all in the loop
Budgets can only ever be set once, at the very start, and never adjusted
Alerts must always be configured before any usage is ever measured
items.explanation: Setting the budget and alert against the freshly right-sized baseline means the alert actually reflects the corrected, intended spend level — setting it against the old over-provisioned number would just enshrine the waste as the new normal.
items.reference:
🔁 measure → right-size → budget-alert → re-audit → (repeat)

Why: A loop only works if every step, including the repeat, actually happens.

items.prompt: According to L2's waste-pattern table, what is the recommended fix for 'idle/forgotten resources'?
choices: Tag resources with an owner and an expiry, and automate teardown or a recurring review

🗑️ Idle → tag owner + expiry, automate teardown
🛡️ 'Just in case' → right-size against real data, on a schedule

items.reference:

🔁 measure → right-size → budget-alert → re-audit → (repeat)

items.prompt: In `recommendSize`, why does the function take the max of peak CPU and peak memory percent as the 'binding' peak, instead of using CPU alone?
choices: A resource is only as capable as its most constrained dimension, so sizing off just CPU could ignore memory actually being closer to saturation
Memory usage is always higher than CPU usage, so using CPU would be redundant
CPU percent isn't a real measurable quantity in cloud monitoring
It's arbitrary and could just as correctly use CPU alone
items.explanation: If memory peaks higher relative to its own limits than CPU does, sizing off CPU alone would recommend a vCPU count that ignores the dimension actually closest to running out — taking the max ensures the recommendation accounts for whichever resource is the real constraint.
items.reference:
💻 bindingPeak = max(cpuPercent, memoryPercent)
🎯 impliedVcpu = currentVcpu × bindingPeak / targetBand

Why: The most constrained dimension determines real capacity, not the average of both.

items.prompt: `recommendSize` rounds `impliedVcpu` up (`Math.ceil`) rather than to the nearest whole number. Why round up specifically?
choices: Rounding down could under-provision below the calculated need, since a fraction of a vCPU isn't purchasable — rounding up guarantees at least the calculated capacity
Rounding up always produces a cheaper recommendation
Math.ceil is required by the TypeScript type system for this calculation
It has no effect since impliedVcpu is always already a whole number
items.explanation: Since only whole vCPU counts are purchasable, rounding down would silently under-provision relative to the calculated target; rounding up ensures the recommendation never falls short of the number the calculation actually determined was needed.
items.reference:
💻 bindingPeak = max(cpuPercent, memoryPercent)
🎯 impliedVcpu = currentVcpu × bindingPeak / targetBand

Why: The most constrained dimension determines real capacity, not the average of both.

items.prompt: `forecastSpend` flags a resource at $8,000 of a $10,000 budget by day 10 of 30 as 'over-budget-forecast,' even though $8,000 is still technically under $10,000. Why?
choices: The straight-line daily rate ($800/day) projected to the full 30-day period forecasts $24,000, well past the budget, even though today's raw total hasn't crossed it yet
The function has a bug and should not flag this case
$8,000 alone is always considered over budget regardless of the period
The forecast ignores daysElapsed entirely and only looks at spendSoFarUsd
items.explanation: The whole point of a forecast-based check is catching the trajectory, not just the current total — projecting the observed $800/day rate across the full 30-day period yields $24,000, 240% of budget, which is exactly the kind of early warning a spend-so-far-only check would miss.
items.reference:
📉 dailyRate = spendSoFar / daysElapsed
🔮 forecast = dailyRate × periodDays

Why: A forecast catches the trajectory before the raw total confirms the problem.

items.prompt: Why does `forecastSpend` use a straight-line daily average across the whole elapsed period, rather than only the most recent day or two?
choices: It's the simplest model, but it's slower to react to a sudden recent rate change since it dilutes a new spike with many prior lower-spend days — a trailing-window version would react faster
A straight-line average always reacts faster to sudden changes than a trailing window would
It's the only mathematically valid way to forecast future spend
It has no effect on how quickly the forecast reacts to a rate change
items.explanation: Averaging over the whole elapsed period blends in many prior, lower-spend days with a sudden recent spike, so the forecast rises more slowly than the actual current rate — a trailing-window version (like a short-window burn-rate check) would surface a sudden change faster.
items.reference:
📉 dailyRate = spendSoFar / daysElapsed
🔮 forecast = dailyRate × periodDays

Why: A forecast catches the trajectory before the raw total confirms the problem.

✂️ Trim too far → no margin for a real spike → outage
🔒 Ceiling too low → legit spike gets capped → outage

Why: Cost and reliability are a real tension, not a one-sided optimization.

items.prompt: What real failure can result from setting an auto-scaling ceiling too low purely to control cost?

The ceiling has no effect on reliability, only on the monthly bill
Setting a ceiling always improves both cost and reliability with no trade-off
A low ceiling guarantees the resource can never experience a traffic spike
items.explanation: An auto-scaling ceiling set too low to control cost can turn a real, legitimate traffic spike into an outage, since the system is prevented from scaling to actually absorb the load — the cost guardrail becomes the cause of the very kind of incident reliability tracking exists to prevent.
items.reference:
✂️ Trim too far → no margin for a real spike → outage
🔒 Ceiling too low → legit spike gets capped → outage

Why: Cost and reliability are a real tension, not a one-sided optimization.

items.prompt: L3 asks what changes if usage is highly seasonal (a predictable end-of-month spike) rather than steady. Why does forecastSpend's straight-line daily average handle that case poorly?
choices: It would misread a legitimate, expected spike late in the period as a budget overrun, or conversely miss that an average early-period rate understates a predictable later surge — a comparison against the same point in a typical cycle would be more accurate
Seasonal usage has no effect on forecasting accuracy at all
forecastSpend already accounts for seasonality via the periodDays parameter
Seasonal usage only affects right-sizing, never budget forecasting
items.explanation: A straight-line average blends a predictable seasonal pattern into a single flat rate, so it can't distinguish 'this is the expected end-of-month spike' from 'this is a genuine runaway trend' — comparing against the equivalent point in a prior, similar cycle handles that distinction the average alone cannot.
items.reference:
📅 Seasonal usage → compare to the same point in a prior cycle
👥 Shared/multi-tenant → allocate savings/spend proportionally by usage

Why: The worked example is one case, not the whole territory these tools need to cover.

items.prompt: L3 also asks what changes if the resource being right-sized is shared across five teams' workloads. Why can't the recommendSize and monthlySavings numbers be used directly by any one team in that case?

Shared resources can never be right-sized at all, only single-tenant ones can
The calculator produces a different, incorrect formula automatically for shared resources
Shared resources have no measurable utilization data to work from
items.explanation: recommendSize and monthlySavings are built assuming one team owns a resource's full cost and usage; on a shared resource, right-sizing the whole cluster is still valid, but attributing the resulting savings or overrun to a specific team requires an extra allocation step, usually proportional to each team's share of usage.
items.reference:
📅 Seasonal usage → compare to the same point in a prior cycle
👥 Shared/multi-tenant → allocate savings/spend proportionally by usage

Why: The worked example is one case, not the whole territory these tools need to cover.

items.prompt: Complete `impliedVcpu(currentVcpu, bindingPeakPercent, targetPercent)` so it returns `currentVcpu * bindingPeakPercent / targetPercent`, rounded up to the nearest whole number (never below 1). Throw an Error if `targetPercent` is not greater than 0.

tests.description: 8 vCPU, 10% peak, 65% target -> 2 vCPU (rounds up, never below 1)

items.explanation: This scales the currently-provisioned vCPU count by the ratio of the observed binding peak to the target utilization band, then rounds up (since fractional vCPUs aren't purchasable) and floors at 1 (since a recommendation of zero capacity is never valid).
items.reference:
💻 bindingPeak = max(cpuPercent, memoryPercent)
🎯 impliedVcpu = currentVcpu × bindingPeak / targetBand

Why: The most constrained dimension determines real capacity, not the average of both.

items.prompt: Complete `impliedVcpu(currentVcpu, bindingPeakPercent, targetPercent)` so it returns `currentVcpu * bindingPeakPercent / targetPercent`, rounded up to the nearest whole number (never below 1). Throw an Error if `currentVcpu` is not greater than 0.
items.explanation: A currently-provisioned vCPU count of zero or below is never a valid input to scale from, so validating it up front prevents a nonsensical recommendation from being computed off an invalid baseline.

items.prompt: Complete `monthlySavings(currentVcpu, currentMonthlyCostUsd, recommendedVcpu)` so it returns the savings in dollars, rounded to 2 decimal places: cost-per-vCPU times the vCPUs removed. Throw an Error if `currentVcpu` is not greater than 0.

tests.description: recommended vCPU equal to current -> $0 saved

items.explanation: Deriving a per-vCPU cost from the current provisioning lets the savings scale linearly with however many vCPUs the recommendation removes, which is what turns a sizing recommendation into a concrete dollar figure a team can act on.
items.reference:
💰 costPerVcpu = currentCost / currentVcpu
➖ savings = (currentVcpu − recommendedVcpu) × costPerVcpu

Why: A recommendation only becomes actionable once it's translated into real dollars.

items.prompt: Complete `forecastMonthEnd(spendSoFarUsd, daysElapsed, periodDays)` so it returns the forecasted total spend for the full period, rounded to 2 decimal places: `(spendSoFarUsd / daysElapsed) * periodDays`. Throw an Error if `daysElapsed` is not greater than 0.

tests.description: $8000 spent by day 10 of a 30-day period -> $24000 forecasted
$3000 spent by day 10 of a 30-day period -> $9000 forecasted

items.explanation: Projecting the observed daily spend rate forward across the full period is what catches a bad trajectory early — waiting for spendSoFarUsd alone to exceed the budget would mean finding out only after the damage is already done.
items.reference:
📉 dailyRate = spendSoFar / daysElapsed
🔮 forecast = dailyRate × periodDays

Why: A forecast catches the trajectory before the raw total confirms the problem.

items.explanation: A period of zero or negative days has no meaningful forecast to project, so validating it up front prevents a nonsensical or misleading result from ever being returned to a caller.

items.prompt: Complete `severityFor(percentOfBudgetForecasted)` so it returns `'over-budget-forecast'` when the forecast is 110% of budget or more, `'watch'` when it's 95% or more (but under 110%), and `'on-track'` otherwise.
items.explanation: The two thresholds separate 'trending over budget, act now' from 'trending close, worth watching' from 'currently fine' — checked from the highest threshold down so a forecast at or above 110% is never mistakenly caught by the lower 'watch' branch first.
items.reference:
✅ <95% → on-track
⚠️ 95-109% → watch
🚨 ≥110% → over-budget-forecast

Why: A tiered threshold avoids both false calm and alert fatigue.
